 Download 
You may download ASCII files which contain all the values of radius, ratio etc. by using the links
given in the table header below.
 
All coordinates of all packings are packed as ASCII files
 here .
 
All packings are stored as nice PDF files
 here .
 
All contact graphs of all packings are stored as nice PDF files
 here .
 
  
For industrial applications, for instance if a machine has to do an important job at every sphere center,
 
it is useful to know a tour visiting each of the sphere centers once which is of minimal length.
 
This problem is known as the "Traveling Salesman Problem" (TSP).
Thus (very near) optimal tours are provided for every packing.
 
All optimal TSP tours of all packings are stored as nice PDF files
 here .
-->
 
 
 

 
 Results 
The table below summarizes the current status of the search.
 
Please use the links in the following table to view a picture for a certain configuration.
 
Furthermore, note that for certain values of N several distinct optimal configurations exist;
however, only one is shown here.
 
 Proven optimal packings are indicated by a radius in bold face type.
 
 
 Legend: 
 
 N the number of spheres; colors correspond to active researchers in the past, see "References" at the bottom of the page
 radius of the spheres in the cube
 distance packing of spheres in a cube is equivalent to distributing points in a cube; the latter are then the sphere centers. "distance" is here the greatest distance of these points
 ratio = 1/radius
 density ratio of total volume occupied by the spheres to container volume (for an infinite face-centered cubic packing
you get the well-known value ρ = Pi/(3*sqrt(2))=0.74048048969)
 contacts number of contacts between circles and container and between the circles themselves, respectively
 loose number of circles that have still degrees of freedom for a movement inside the container (so called "rattlers")
 boundary number of circles that have contact to the container (rattlers too if possible)
 symmetry group of the packing (Schönfliess notation); if field is empty then the packing has symmetry element C 1 
-->
 reference for the best known packing so far

 Formulae 
The following table contains parameters from least-square fits of the ratio R/r over N by an exponential law
R/r = a * N^b. This means that the least-square fit was applied to the function log(R/r) = b * log(N) + log(a)
which gives also the standard deviation s_(n-1).
 
Please note that the fits are taken from different intervals of N. Remember this if you like to extrapolate 
the given formulae to higher values of N.
 
 
 
 Interval of fit a b s
 11...100 1.232962 0.476521 0.005844
 101...200 1.207426 0.481650 0.001398
 201...300 1.212083 0.481106 0.001169
 301...400 1.176876 0.486370 0.000915
 401...500 1.217405 0.480678 0.001356

 21...500 1.203885 0.482409 0.002347
 101...500 1.195318 0.483673 0.001265
 201...500 1.193373 0.483954 0.001196
 301...500 1.199264 0.483144 0.001176
 
 
 
-->

 
 Applications 
Suppose, you have to cut circles with a fixed diameter from a square-shaped plate of any material with fixed side length.
 
How many circles can you get in order to minimize the waste?
 
Please use the following form for this calculation:
 
 
 
 
 Side length of square-shaped plate:      
 (enter only numbers , no units and/or text please)
 Diameter of small circles:      
 (no units please)
 
-->
 
 
 
Suppose, you have to cut a fixed number of circles with a fixed diameter from a square-shaped plate of any material.
 
What is the minimum side length of the square?
 
Please use the following form for this calculation:
 
 
 
 
 Diameter of small circles:      
 (no units please)
 Number of small circles:      
 (enter only numbers , no units and/or text please)
 
 
 
-->
 
Please enter your name and your e-mail address in the following forms. I can assure you that your data won't be misused for any purposes.
 
 Name:       e-mail-address: 
 
 
 
 
-->
 
A recently discovered application was inspired by Dennis Gretsinger: How to measure large holes with small gauge pins .
 
Feel free to send me an e-mail for comments and suggestions!
 
 
 

 
 Related entries in the OEIS 
(On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences) 
 
 A084618 
 Maximum number of circles with area 1 that can be packed in a circle of area n 
 A084619 
 Maximum number of circles of radius 1 that can be packed in a circle of radius n 
 A084644 
 Best packings of m >1 equal circles into a larger circle setting a new density record
 
Many thanks to Hugo Pfoertner for establishing these sequences.

 09-Apr-2012: The last of Goldberg's packings (up to one million of spheres) for N =1000188 and 1024192 are now shown here [31].
 
 09-Apr-2012: As it is easy to see there are many candidate packings which are derived from higher packings (i.e. from a
"root" packing with a higher number of spheres) only by omitting one or more spheres. If they have exactly the same radius as the root packing and
were not discovered before I have decided to give the credits who owns them for the associated root packing. According to this rule David W. Cantrell
and I have calculated some improvements compared to the old packings shown here for N =146, 174, 179, 188, 189, 201, 235, 236, 237, 238, 239, 240,
241, 255, 257, 361–364, 408–415, 489–499, 564–566, 653–665, 721–725 and 857–863.
 
 09-Apr-2012: They same once more for N =619–628, 630, 636, 637, 641–652 and 707–720.
 
 09-Apr-2012: Here are derivatives from two more roots: N =793–799 by David W. Cantrell
and N =895–935 by Eckard Specht.
 
 09-Apr-2012: David W. Cantrell sent me four packings, namely for N =220, 445, 786 and 1008, which are
members of a particularly nice family in which spheres are grouped in pyramids in four corners of the cube and in a tetrahedron in the
middle of the cube. I have calculated all derivatives from these roots in the ranges N =211–219, 428–444, 733–785,
937–1007 which are better than the previous ones.

 12-Apr-2012: The range between N =501 and 600 was reconsidered, improvements for N =501–538, 551–563,
568–582 and 593–599 were found by Eckard Specht [31]. 
 
 13-Apr-2012: Six improvements for N =64, 69, 122, 125, 132 and 146 by WenQi Huang and Liang Yu [27].
 
 15-Apr-2012: The range between N =200 and 299 was reconsidered, nearly for all of the non-regular packings and its

 15-Apr-2012: A new family of packings was discovered by David W. Cantrell [24] which typical roots are N =122, 395,
538, 711 and 918. Their derivatives are N = 394–385, 537–530, 710–685 and 917–886. David sent me two (may be the final)
improvements for N =64 and 69.

164, 179, 181, 182, 183, 188, 189, 193, 194 by Eckard Specht [31].
 
 21-Apr-2012: A third new family of packings was discovered by David W. Cantrell [24] which roots are N =n^2 (n+1) / 2.
Improvements were found for N =405 (and 404 as its derivative) and the new packing for N =1470. David sent me two improvements for
 N =92 and 93.

by Eckard Specht [31].

470, 471, 472, 474, 477, 479, 584, 586, 602, 605, 619, 620, 621, 622, 623, 624, 625, 626, 627, 628, 630, 632, 634, 635, 636, 637, 638, 639, 673, 788,
812 and 879 by Eckard Specht [31]. Now all packings shown here fulfill the unproven conjecture that the radius r ( N ) as a function of
 N is a monoton decreasing function (but not a strictly monoton decreasing function!).
